author: Corvin Avellus, Surveyor of the Imperial Highways
pages:
#On the Old Roads

I have spent twenty-two years walking the roads of the north with a measuring chain, a pot of red paint and a mule named Patience who has none. I offer these notes to fellow travellers, so that they may understand the stones beneath their boots.

#The Three Kinds of Road

The oldest roads were laid by the first Nordic kings. They are narrow, they climb straight over hills rather than going around them, and they are paved with flat stones set on edge. The kings did not care whether you arrived tired, only that you arrived.

The second kind are the cobbled highways built during the occupation by southern legions. These are wide, well drained and gently graded, and the Nords complain about them constantly while using them every day.

The third kind are the paths that simply happened: deer trails widened by carts, shortcuts that became habits. These are the most dangerous, for they lead wherever the first fool who walked them wanted to go.

#Mileposts and Their Meanings

Along the legion roads you will find carved posts at regular intervals. A post with one notch marks a mile. A post with a carved shield marks a place where a patrol is supposed to be stationed, though in my experience the patrol is usually elsewhere.

A post painted red is my own work. It means the bridge ahead is unsafe. Please believe the paint.

#Things the Road Will Not Tell You

Bandits favour the narrow places where a road passes between rocks. Wolves favour the edges of forests at dusk. Trolls favour any cave within sight of a road, because travellers are slower than elk and complain more audibly.

If you find a road that seems to lead somewhere important but is overgrown and forgotten, be careful. There is usually a reason a road was abandoned, and the reason is usually still there.
